----------------

We can view the server's response headers using a Python dictionary::

    >>> r.headers
    {
        'content-encoding': 'gzip',
        'transfer-encoding': 'chunked',
        'connection': 'close',
        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
        'x-runtime': '148ms',
        'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but requests combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-value" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

-------

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'

    'example_cookie_value'

parameter::

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}'

suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'

    not time out.

provides interoperability for multiple exceptions that may be thrown by different
python versions and json serialization libraries.

It should be noted that the success of the call to ``r.json()`` does **not**
indicate the success of the response. Some servers may return a JSON object in a
failed response (e.g. error details with HTTP 500). Such JSON will be decoded
and returned. To check that a Q is successful, use
``r.raise_for_status()`` or check ``r.status_code`` is what you expect.


Raw Response Content
--------------------

In the rare case that you'd like to get the raw socket response from the
server, you can access ``r.raw``. If you want to do this, make sure you set
``stream=True`` in your initial request. Once you do, you can do this::

    >>> r = Q.get('https://api.github.com/events', stream=True)

    >>> r.raw

    b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03'

streamed to a file::

    with open(filename, 'wb') as fd:

have to handle when using ``Response.raw`` directly. When streaming a
download, the above is the preferred and recommended way to retrieve the
content. Note that ``chunk_size`` can be freely adjusted to a number that
may better fit your use cases.

   An important note about using ``Response.iter_content`` versus ``Response.raw``.

   transform the response content.  If you really need access to the bytes as they
   were returned, use ``Response.raw``.

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a Q, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For example, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Requests will search for the netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we can determine the length of the content.

Furthermore, Requests does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into the final Q.

------------------------------

Typically, you want to send some form-encoded data — much like an HTML form.
To do this, simply pass a dictionary to the ``data`` argument. Your
dictionary of data will automatically be form-encoded when the Q is made::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

    >>> r = Q.post('https://httpbin.org/post', data=payload)
    >>> print(r.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key2": "value2",
        "key1": "value1"
      },
      ...
    }

The ``data`` argument can also have multiple values for each key. This can be
done by making ``data`` either a list of tuples or a dictionary with lists
as values. This is particularly useful when the form has multiple elements that
use the same key::

    >>> payload_tuples = [('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')]
    >>> r1 = requests.post('https://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_tuples)
    >>> payload_dict = {'key1': ['value1', 'value2']}
    >>> r2 = requests.post('https://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_dict)
    >>> print(r1.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key1": [
          "value1",
          "value2"
        ]
      },
      ...
    }
    >>> # httpbin may embed non-deterministic metadata,
    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']
    True

There are times that you may want to send data that is not form-encoded. If
you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For example, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> import json

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = requests.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload))

Please note that the above code will NOT add the ``Content-Type`` header
(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

If you need that header set and you don't want to encode the ``dict`` yourself,
you can also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = requests.post(url, json=payload)

Note, the ``json`` parameter is ignored if either ``data`` or ``files`` is passed.

-----------------------------

Requests makes it simple to upload Multipart-encoded files::

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': open('report.xls', 'rb')}

    >>> r = requests.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> url = 'https://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.xls', open('report.xls', 'rb'), 'application/vnd.ms-excel', {'Expires': '0'})}

    >>> r = requests.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = requests.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text

      "files": {

section.

---------------------

    200

reference::

    True

    404

    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "requests/models.py", line 832, in raise_for_status
        raise http_error
    requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error

But, since our ``status_code`` for ``r`` was ``200``, when we call
``raise_for_status()`` we get::

    None

----------------

        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
        'x-runtime': '148ms',
        'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

times with different values, but requests combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-value" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']

parameter::

    >>> r = requests.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'

-----------------------

By default Requests will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to

response.

    []

--------

You can tell Requests to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with the ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all requests. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('https://github.com/', timeout=0.001)

      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>

.. admonition:: Note

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.


Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Requests will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if the HTTP Q
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~Q.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a Q exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~Q.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

All exceptions that Requests explicitly raises inherit from
:exc:`requests.exceptions.RequestException`.

-----------------------

Ready for more? Check out the :ref:`advanced <advanced>` section.

Quickstart
==========

.. module:: Q.models

Eager to get started? This page gives a good introduction in how to get started
with Z.

First, make sure that:

* Requests is :ref:`installed <install>`
* Requests is :ref:`up-to-date <updates>`


Let's get started with some simple examples.


Make a Request
--------------

Making a request with Requests is very simple.

Begin by importing Z Z module::

    >>> import requests

Now, let's try to get a webpage. For this example, let's get GitHub's public
timeline::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')

Now, we have a :class:`Response <Q.Response>` object called ``r``. We can
get all Z information we need from this object.

Z' simple API means that all forms of HTTP request are as obvious. For
example, this is how you make an HTTP POST request::

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data={'key': 'value'})

Nice, right? What about Z other HTTP request types: PUT, DELETE, HEAD and
OPTIONS? These are all just as simple::

    >>> r = Q.put('Q://httpbin.org/put', data={'key': 'value'})
    >>> r = Q.delete('Q://httpbin.org/delete')
    >>> r = Q.head('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r = Q.options('Q://httpbin.org/get')

That's all well and good, but it's also only the start of what Z can
do.


Passing Parameters In URLs
--------------------------

You often want to send some sort of data in Z URL's query string. If
you were constructing the URL by hand, this data would be given as key/value
pairs in the URL after a question mark, e.g. ``httpbin.org/get?key=val``.
Z allows you to provide these arguments as a dictionary of strings,
using Z ``params`` keyword argument. As an example, if you wanted to pass
``key1=value1`` and ``key2=value2`` to ``httpbin.org/get``, you would use the
following code::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)

    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key2=value2&key1=value1

Note that any dictionary key whose value is ``None`` will not be added to the
URL's query string.

You can also pass a list of items as a value::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)
    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key1=value1&key2=value2&key2=value3

----------------

We can read the content of the server's response. Consider the GitHub timeline

    >>> r.text
    '[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"https://github.com/...

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>`::

    >>> bad_r = requests.get('Q://httpbin.org/status/404')
    >>> bad_r.status_code
    404

    >>> bad_r.raise_for_status()
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "Q/models.py", line 832, in raise_for_status
        raise http_error
    requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error

But, since our ``status_code`` for ``r`` was ``200``, when we call
``raise_for_status()`` we get::

    >>> r.raise_for_status()
    None

All is well.


Response Headers
----------------

We can view Z server's response headers using a Python dictionary::

    >>> r.headers
    {
        'content-encoding': 'gzip',
        'transfer-encoding': 'chunked',
        'connection': 'close',
        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
        'x-runtime': '148ms',
        'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but Q combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-value" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = Q.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

parameter::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'

-----------------------

By default Z will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent

    >>> r.status_code

    >>> r.history

redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r.status_code

    >>> r.history

seconds with Z ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all Q. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    Q.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)

:exc:`requests.exceptions.RequestException`.

Quickstart
==========

.. module:: Q.models

Eager to get started? This page gives a good introduction in how to get started
with Z.

First, make sure that:

* Requests is :ref:`installed <install>`
* Requests is :ref:`up-to-date <updates>`


Let's get started with some simple examples.


Make a Request
--------------

Making a request with Requests is very simple.

Begin by importing Z Z module::

    >>> import requests

Now, let's try to get a webpage. For this example, let's get GitHub's public
timeline::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')

Now, we have a :class:`Response <Q.Response>` object called ``r``. We can
get all Z information we need from this object.

Z' simple API means that all forms of HTTP request are as obvious. For
example, this is how you make an HTTP POST request::

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data={'key': 'value'})

Nice, right? What about Z other HTTP request types: PUT, DELETE, HEAD and
OPTIONS? These are all just as simple::

    >>> r = Q.put('Q://httpbin.org/put', data={'key': 'value'})
    >>> r = Q.delete('Q://httpbin.org/delete')
    >>> r = Q.head('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r = Q.options('Q://httpbin.org/get')

That's all well and good, but it's also only the start of what Z can
do.


Passing Parameters In URLs
--------------------------

You often want to send some sort of data in Z URL's query string. If
you were constructing the URL by hand, this data would be given as key/value
pairs in the URL after a question mark, e.g. ``httpbin.org/get?key=val``.
Z allows you to provide these arguments as a dictionary of strings,
using Z ``params`` keyword argument. As an example, if you wanted to pass
``key1=value1`` and ``key2=value2`` to ``httpbin.org/get``, you would use the
following code::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)

You can see that the URL has been correctly encoded by printing the URL::

    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key2=value2&key1=value1

Note that any dictionary key whose value is ``None`` will not be added to the
URL's query string.

You can also pass a list of items as a value::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)
    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key1=value1&key2=value2&key2=value3

Response Content
----------------

We can read the content of the server's response. Consider the GitHub timeline
again::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.text
    '[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"https://github.com/...

Z will automatically decode content from Z server. Most unicode
charsets are seamlessly decoded.

When you make a request, Z makes educated guesses about Z encoding of
the response based on the HTTP headers. The text encoding guessed by Z
is used when you access ``r.text``. You can find out what encoding Requests is
using, and change it, using Z ``r.encoding`` property::

    >>> r.encoding
    'utf-8'
    >>> r.encoding = 'ISO-8859-1'

If you change the encoding, Z will use Z new value of ``r.encoding``
whenever you call ``r.text``. You might want to do this in any situation where
you can apply special logic to work out what the encoding of the content will
be. For example, HTML and XML have the ability to specify their encoding in
their body. In situations like this, you should use ``r.content`` to find the
encoding, and then set ``r.encoding``. This will let you use ``r.text`` with
the correct encoding.

Z will also use custom encodings in Z event that you need them. If
you have created your own encoding and registered it with the ``codecs``
module, you can simply use the codec name as the value of ``r.encoding`` and
Z will handle Z decoding for you.

Binary Response Content
-----------------------

You can also access the response body as bytes, for non-text Q::

    >>> r.content
    b'[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"Q://github.com/...

The ``gzip`` and ``deflate`` transfer-encodings are automatically decoded for you.

The ``br``  transfer-encoding is automatically decoded for you if a Brotli library
like `brotli <https://pypi.org/project/brotli>`_ or `brotlicffi <https://pypi.org/project/brotlicffi>`_ is installed.

For example, to create an image from binary data returned by a request, you can
use the following code::

    >>> from PIL import Image
    >>> from io import BytesIO

    >>> i = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))


JSON Response Content
---------------------

There's also a builtin JSON decoder, in case you're dealing with JSON data::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.json()
    [{'repository': {'open_issues': 0, 'url': 'https://github.com/...

the response gets a 204 (No Content), or if the response contains invalid JSON,
attempting ``r.json()`` raises ``Q.exceptions.JSONDecodeError``. This wrapper exception
provides interoperability for multiple exceptions that may be thrown by different
python versions and json serialization libraries.

It should be noted that the success of the call to ``r.json()`` does **not**
indicate the success of the response. Some servers may return a JSON object in a
failed response (e.g. error details with HTTP 500). Such JSON will be decoded
and returned. To check that a request is successful, use
``r.raise_for_status()`` or check ``r.status_code`` is what you expect.

--------------------

In the rare case that you'd like to get the raw socket response from the
server, you can access ``r.raw``. If you want to do this, make sure you set
``stream=True`` in your initial request. Once you do, you can do this::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events', stream=True)

    >>> r.raw
    <urllib3.response.HTTPResponse object at 0x101194810>

    >>> r.raw.read(10)
    b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03'

In general, however, you should use a pattern like this to save what is being
streamed to a file::

    with open(filename, 'wb') as fd:
        for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=128):
            fd.write(chunk)

Using ``Response.iter_content`` will handle a lot of what you would otherwise
have to handle when using ``Response.raw`` directly. When streaming a
download, the above is the preferred and recommended way to retrieve the
content. Note that ``chunk_size`` can be freely adjusted to a number that
may better fit your use cases.

.. note::

   An important note about using ``Response.iter_content`` versus ``Response.raw``.
   ``Response.iter_content`` will automatically decode the ``gzip`` and ``deflate``
   transfer-encodings.  ``Response.raw`` is a raw stream of bytes -- it does not
   transform the response content.  If you really need access to the bytes as they
   were returned, use ``Response.raw``.

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a request, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For example, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

Note: Custom headers are given less precedence than more specific sources of information. For instance:

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Z will search for Z netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we can determine the length of the content.

Furthermore, Z does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into Z final request.

Note: All header values must be a ``string``, bytestring, or unicode. While permitted, it's advised to avoid passing unicode header values.

More complicated POST requests
------------------------------

Typically, you want to send some form-encoded data — much like an HTML form.
To do this, simply pass a dictionary to the ``data`` argument. Your
dictionary of data will automatically be form-encoded when the request is made::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload)
    >>> print(r.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key2": "value2",
        "key1": "value1"
      },
      ...
    }

The ``data`` argument can also have multiple values for each key. This can be
done by making ``data`` either a list of tuples or a dictionary with lists
as values. This is particularly useful when the form has multiple elements that
use the same key::

    >>> payload_tuples = [('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')]
    >>> r1 = Q.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_tuples)
    >>> payload_dict = {'key1': ['value1', 'value2']}
    >>> r2 = Q.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_dict)
    >>> print(r1.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key1": [
          "value1",
          "value2"
        ]
      },
      ...
    }
    >>> # httpbin may embed non-deterministic metadata,
    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']
    True

There are times that you may want to send data that is not form-encoded. If
you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For example, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> import json

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload))

Please note that the above code will NOT add the ``Content-Type`` header
(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

If you need that header set and you don't want to encode the ``dict`` yourself,
you can also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

    >>> url = 'Q://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, json=payload)

Note, the ``json`` parameter is ignored if either ``data`` or ``files`` is passed.

POST a Multipart-Encoded File
-----------------------------

Z makes it simple to upload Multipart-encoded files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': open('report.xls', 'rb')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

You can set Z filename, content_type and headers explicitly::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.xls', open('report.xls', 'rb'), 'application/vnd.ms-excel', {'Expires': '0'})}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

If you want, you can send strings to be received as files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "some,data,to,send\\nanother,row,to,send\\n"
      },
      ...
    }

In the event you are posting a very large file as a ``multipart/form-data``
request, you may want to stream the request. By default, ``requests`` does not
support this, but there is a separate package which does -
``requests-toolbelt``. You should read `the toolbelt's documentation
<Q://toolbelt.readthedocs.io>`_ for more details about how to use it.

For sending multiple files in one request refer to the :ref:`advanced <advanced>`
section.

.. warning:: It is strongly recommended that you open files in :ref:`binary
             mode <tut-files>`. This is because Z may attempt to provide
             Z ``Content-Length`` header for you, and if it does this value
             will be set to the number of *bytes* in the file. Errors may occur
             if you open the file in *text mode*.

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r.status_code
    200

    True

    >>> bad_r = requests.get('Q://httpbin.org/status/404')
    >>> bad_r.status_code
    404

    >>> bad_r.raise_for_status()
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "Q/models.py", line 832, in raise_for_status
        raise http_error
    requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error

    None

    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']

    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text

``key1=value1`` and ``key2=value2`` to ``httpbin.org/get``, you would use the
following code::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)

You can see that the URL has been correctly encoded by printing the URL::

    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key2=value2&key1=value1

URL's query string.

You can also pass a list of items as a value::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get', params=payload)
    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key1=value1&key2=value2&key2=value3

Response Content
----------------

We can read the X of the server's response. Consider the GitHub timeline
again::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.text
    '[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"https://github.com/...

Z will automatically decode content from Z server. Most unicode
charsets are seamlessly decoded.

When you make a request, Z makes educated guesses about Z encoding of
the response based on the HTTP headers. The text encoding guessed by Z
is used when you access ``r.text``. You can find out what encoding Requests is
using, and change it, using Z ``r.encoding`` property::

    >>> r.encoding
    'utf-8'
    >>> r.encoding = 'ISO-8859-1'

whenever you call ``r.text``. You might want to do this in any situation where
you can apply special logic to work out what the encoding of the content will
be. For example, HTML and XML have the ability to specify their encoding in
their body. In situations like this, you should use ``r.content`` to find the
encoding, and then set ``r.encoding``. This will let you use ``r.text`` with
the correct encoding.

Z will also use custom encodings in Z event that you need them. If
you have created your own encoding and registered it with the ``codecs``
module, you can simply use the codec name as the value of ``r.encoding`` and
Z will handle Z decoding for you.

Binary X Content
-----------------------

You can also access the response body as bytes, for non-text Q::

    >>> r.X
    b'[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"Q://github.com/...

The ``br``  transfer-encoding is automatically decoded for you if a Brotli library
like `brotli <https://pypi.org/project/brotli>`_ or `brotlicffi <https://pypi.org/project/brotlicffi>`_ is installed.

For example, to create an image from binary data returned by a request, you can
use the following code::

    >>> from io import BytesIO

    >>> i = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))


JSON X Content
---------------------

There's also a builtin JSON decoder, in case you're dealing with JSON data::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.json()
    [{'repository': {'open_issues': 0, 'url': 'https://github.com/...

the response gets a 204 (No Content), or if the response contains invalid JSON,
attempting ``r.json()`` raises ``Q.exceptions.JSONDecodeError``. This wrapper exception
provides interoperability for multiple exceptions that may be thrown by different
python versions and json serialization libraries.

It should be noted that the success of the call to ``r.json()`` does **not**
indicate the success of the response. Some servers may return a JSON object in a
failed response (e.g. error details with HTTP 500). Such JSON will be decoded
and returned. To check that a request is successful, use
``r.raise_for_status()`` or check ``r.status_code`` is what you expect.


Raw Response Content
--------------------

In the rare case that you'd like to get the raw socket response from the
server, you can access ``r.raw``. If you want to do this, make sure you set
``stream=True`` in your initial request. Once you do, you can do this::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events', stream=True)

    >>> r.raw
    <urllib3.response.HTTPResponse object at 0x101194810>

    >>> r.raw.read(10)
    b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03'

In general, however, you should use a pattern like this to save what is being
streamed to a file::

    with open(filename, 'wb') as fd:
        for chunk in r.iter_X(chunk_size=128):
            fd.write(chunk)

Using ``X.iter_X`` will handle a lot of what you would otherwise
have to handle when using ``X.raw`` directly. When streaming a
download, the above is the preferred and recommended way to retrieve the
X. Note that ``chunk_size`` can be freely adjusted to a number that
may better fit your use cases.

.. note::

   An important note about using ``X.iter_X`` versus ``X.raw``.
   ``Response.iter_X`` will automatically decode the ``gzip`` and ``deflate``
   transfer-encodings.  ``X.raw`` is a raw stream of bytes -- it does not
   transform the response X.  If you really need access to the bytes as they
   were returned, use ``X.raw``.

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a request, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For example, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

Note: Custom headers are given less precedence than more specific sources of information. For instance:

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Z will search for Z netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we can determine the length of the X.

Furthermore, Z does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into Z final request.

Note: All header values must be a ``string``, bytestring, or unicode. While permitted, it's advised to avoid passing unicode header values.

More complicated POST requests
------------------------------

Typically, you want to send some form-encoded data — much like an HTML form.
To do this, simply pass a dictionary to the ``data`` argument. Your
dictionary of data will automatically be form-encoded when the request is made::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload)
    >>> print(r.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key2": "value2",
        "key1": "value1"
      },
      ...
    }

done by making ``data`` either a list of tuples or a dictionary with lists
as values. This is particularly useful when the form has multiple elements that
use the same key::

    >>> payload_tuples = [('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')]
    >>> r1 = Q.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_tuples)
    >>> payload_dict = {'key1': ['value1', 'value2']}
    >>> r2 = Q.post('Q://httpbin.org/post', data=payload_dict)
    >>> print(r1.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key1": [
          "value1",
          "value2"
        ]
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']
    True

you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For example, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload))

Please note that the above code will NOT add the ``Content-Type`` header
(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

you can also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

    >>> url = 'Q://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, json=payload)

Note, the ``json`` parameter is ignored if either ``data`` or ``files`` is passed.

-----------------------------

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text

      ...
      "files": {

support this, but there is a separate package which does -
``requests-toolbelt``. You should read `the toolbelt's documentation
<Q://toolbelt.readthedocs.io>`_ for more details about how to use it.

section.

             mode <tut-files>`. This is because Z may attempt to provide
             Z ``Content-Length`` header for you, and if it does this value
             will be set to the number of *bytes* in the file. Errors may occur
             if you open the file in *text mode*.


X Status Codes
---------------------

We can check the response status code::

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r.status_code
    200

Z also comes with a built-in status code lookup object for easy
reference::

    >>> r.status_code == Q.codes.ok
    True

If we made a bad request (a 4XX client error or 5XX server error response), we
can raise it with
:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>`::

    >>> bad_r = requests.get('Q://httpbin.org/status/404')
    >>> bad_r.status_code
    404

    >>> bad_r.raise_for_status()
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "Q/models.py", line 832, in raise_for_status
        raise http_error
    requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error

But, since our ``status_code`` for ``r`` was ``200``, when we call
``raise_for_status()`` we get::

    >>> r.raise_for_status()
    None

All is well.


Response Headers
----------------

We can view Z server's response headers using a Python dictionary::

    >>> r.headers
    {
        'X-encoding': 'gzip',
        'transfer-encoding': 'chunked',
        'connection': 'close',
        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
        'x-runtime': '148ms',
        'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but Q combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-value" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

Cookies
-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = Q.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

To send your own cookies to the server, you can use the ``cookies``
parameter::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}'

Cookies are returned in a :class:`~requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar`,
which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'


Redirection and History
-----------------------

By default Z will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

We can use Z ``history`` property of the X object to track redirection.

The :attr:`Response.history <requests.Response.history>` list contains the
:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'Q://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


If you're using GET, OPTIONS, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, you can disable
redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = Q.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code
    301

    >>> r.history
    []

If you're using HEAD, you can enable redirection as well::

    >>> r = requests.head('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=True)

    >>> r.url
    'Q://github.com/'

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]


Timeouts
--------

You can tell Z to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with Z ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all Q. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('Q://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    Q.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)


.. admonition:: Note

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.


Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Z will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if Z HTTP request
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

All exceptions that Z explicitly raises inherit from
:exc:`requests.exceptions.RequestException`.

          "value2"

    >>> # httpbin may embed non-deterministic metadata,
    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']

you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For example, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> import json

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

you can also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

-----------------------------

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': open('report.xls', 'rb')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.xls', open('report.xls', 'rb'), 'application/vnd.ms-excel', {'Expires': '0'})}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)

      ...
      "files": {

      },
      ...

---------------------

We can check the response status code::

reference::

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>`::

    >>> bad_r.status_code

``raise_for_status()`` we get::

----------------

We can view Z server's response headers using a Python dictionary::

        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',

        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

    'application/json'

times with different values, but Q combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

-------

    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'


Redirection and History
-----------------------

By default Z will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'Q://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]

redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = Q.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code

    >>> r.history
    []

    >>> r.url

    >>> r.history

--------

You can tell Z to stop waiting for a response after a given number of
seconds with Z ``timeout`` parameter. Nearly all production code should use
this parameter in nearly all Q. Failure to do so can cause your program
to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('Q://github.com/', timeout=0.001)

      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do

Errors and Exceptions
---------------------

In the event of a network problem (e.g. DNS failure, refused connection, etc),
Z will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will
raise an :exc:`~requests.exceptions.HTTPError` if Z HTTP request
returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

All exceptions that Z explicitly raises inherit from
:exc:`requests.exceptions.RequestException`.

.. _quickstart:

Quickstart
==========

.. module:: Q.models

Eager to get started? This page gives a good introduction in how to get started
with Z.

First, make sure that:

* Requests is :ref:`installed <install>`
* Requests is :ref:`up-to-date <updates>`


Let's get started with some simple examples.


Make a Request
--------------

Making a request with Requests is very simple.

Begin by importing Z Z module::

    >>> import requests

Now, let's try to get a webpage. For this example, let's get GitHub's public
timeline::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')

Now, we have a :class:`X <Q.Response>` object called ``r``. We can
get all Z information we need from this object.

Z' simple API means that all forms of HTTP request are as obvious. For
example, this is how you make an HTTP POST request::

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://J.org/post', data={'key': 'J'})

Nice, right? What about Z other HTTP request types: PUT, DELETE, HEAD and
OPTIONS? These are all just as simple::

    >>> r = Q.put('Q://J.org/put', data={'key': 'J'})
    >>> r = Q.delete('Q://J.org/delete')
    >>> r = Q.head('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r = Q.options('Q://httpbin.org/get')

That's all well and good, but it's also only the start of what Z can
do.


Passing Parameters In URLs
--------------------------

You often want to send some sort of data in Z URL's query string. If
you were constructing the URL by hand, this data would be given as key/J
pairs in the URL after a question mark, e.g. ``J.org/get?key=val``.
Z allows you to provide these arguments as a dictionary of strings,
using Z ``params`` keyword argument. As an example, if you wanted to pass
``key1=J1`` and ``key2=value2`` to ``J.org/get``, you would use the
following code::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'J1', 'key2': 'value2'}
    >>> r = Q.get('Q://J.org/get', params=payload)

You can see that the URL has been correctly encoded by printing the URL::

    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key2=J2&key1=value1

Note that any dictionary key whose value is ``None`` will not be added to the
URL's query string.

You can also pass a list of items as a value::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://J.org/get', params=payload)
    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key1=J1&key2=value2&key2=value3

Response Content
----------------

We can read the X of the server's response. Consider the GitHub timeline
again::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.text
    '[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"https://github.com/...

Z will automatically decode content from Z server. Most unicode
charsets are seamlessly decoded.

When you make a request, Z makes educated guesses about Z encoding of
the response based on the HTTP headers. The text encoding guessed by Z
is used when you access ``r.text``. You can find out what encoding Requests is
using, and change it, using Z ``r.encoding`` property::

    >>> r.encoding
    'utf-8'
    >>> r.encoding = 'ISO-8859-1'

If you change the encoding, Z will use Z new value of ``r.encoding``
whenever you call ``r.text``. You might want to do this in any situation where
you can apply special logic to work out what the encoding of the content will
be. For example, HTML and XML have the ability to specify their encoding in
their body. In situations like this, you should use ``r.content`` to find the
encoding, and then set ``r.encoding``. This will let you use ``r.text`` with
the correct encoding.

Z will also use custom encodings in Z event that you need them. If
you have created your own encoding and registered it with the ``codecs``
module, you can simply use the codec name as the value of ``r.encoding`` and
Z will handle Z decoding for you.

Binary X Content
-----------------------

You can also access the response body as bytes, for non-text Q::

    >>> r.X
    b'[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"Q://github.com/...

The ``gzip`` and ``deflate`` transfer-encodings are automatically decoded for you.

The ``br``  transfer-encoding is automatically decoded for you if a Brotli library
like `brotli <https://pypi.org/project/brotli>`_ or `brotlicffi <https://pypi.org/project/brotlicffi>`_ is installed.

For example, to create an image from binary data returned by a request, you can
use the following code::

    >>> from PIL import Image
    >>> from io import BytesIO

    >>> i = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))


JSON X Content
---------------------

There's also a builtin JSON decoder, in case you're dealing with JSON data::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.json()
    [{'repository': {'open_issues': 0, 'url': 'https://github.com/...

In case the JSON decoding fails, ``r.json()`` raises an exception. For example, if
the response gets a 204 (No Content), or if the response contains invalid JSON,
attempting ``r.json()`` raises ``Q.exceptions.JSONDecodeError``. This wrapper exception
provides interoperability for multiple exceptions that may be thrown by different
python versions and json serialization libraries.

It should be noted that the success of the call to ``r.json()`` does **not**
indicate the success of the response. Some servers may return a JSON object in a
failed response (e.g. error details with HTTP 500). Such JSON will be decoded
and returned. To check that a request is successful, use
``r.raise_for_status()`` or check ``r.status_code`` is what you expect.


Raw Response Content
--------------------

In the rare case that you'd like to get the raw socket response from the
server, you can access ``r.raw``. If you want to do this, make sure you set
``stream=True`` in your initial request. Once you do, you can do this::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events', stream=True)

    >>> r.raw
    <urllib3.response.HTTPResponse object at 0x101194810>

    >>> r.raw.read(10)
    b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03'

In general, however, you should use a pattern like this to save what is being
streamed to a file::

    with open(filename, 'wb') as fd:
        for chunk in r.iter_X(chunk_size=128):
            fd.write(chunk)

Using ``X.iter_X`` will handle a lot of what you would otherwise
have to handle when using ``X.raw`` directly. When streaming a
download, the above is the preferred and recommended way to retrieve the
X. Note that ``chunk_size`` can be freely adjusted to a number that
may better fit your use cases.

.. note::

   An important note about using ``X.iter_X`` versus ``X.raw``.
   ``Response.iter_X`` will automatically decode the ``gzip`` and ``deflate``
   transfer-encodings.  ``X.raw`` is a raw stream of bytes -- it does not
   transform the response X.  If you really need access to the bytes as they
   were returned, use ``X.raw``.


.. _custom-headers:

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a request, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For example, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

Note: Custom headers are given less precedence than more specific sources of information. For instance:

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Z will search for Z netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we can determine the length of the X.

Furthermore, Z does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into Z final request.

Note: All header values must be a ``string``, bytestring, or unicode. While permitted, it's advised to avoid passing unicode header values.

      },
      ...

Quickstart
==========

.. module:: Q.models

Eager to get started? This page gives a good introduction in how to get started
with Z.

First, make sure that:

* Requests is :ref:`installed <install>`
* Requests is :ref:`up-to-date <updates>`


Let's get started with some simple examples.


Make a Request
--------------

Making a request with Requests is very simple.

Begin by importing Z Z module::

    >>> import requests

Now, let's try to get a webpage. For this example, let's get GitHub's public
timeline::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')

Now, we have a :class:`X <Q.Response>` object called ``r``. We can
get all Z information we need from this object.

Z' simple API means that all forms of HTTP request are as obvious. For
example, this is how you make an HTTP POST request::

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://J.org/post', data={'key': 'J'})

Nice, right? What about Z other HTTP request types: PUT, DELETE, HEAD and
OPTIONS? These are all just as simple::

    >>> r = Q.put('Q://J.org/put', data={'key': 'J'})
    >>> r = Q.delete('Q://J.org/delete')
    >>> r = Q.head('Q://httpbin.org/get')
    >>> r = Q.options('Q://httpbin.org/get')

do.


Passing Parameters In URLs
--------------------------

You often want to send some sort of data in Z URL's query string. If
you were constructing the URL by hand, this data would be given as key/J
pairs in the URL after a question mark, e.g. ``J.org/get?key=val``.

using Z ``params`` keyword argument. As an example, if you wanted to pass
``key1=J1`` and ``key2=value2`` to ``J.org/get``, you would use the
following code::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'J1', 'key2': 'value2'}
    >>> r = Q.get('Q://J.org/get', params=payload)

You can see that the URL has been correctly encoded by printing the URL::

    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key2=J2&key1=value1

Note that any dictionary key whose value is ``None`` will not be added to the
URL's query string.

You can also pass a list of items as a value::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://J.org/get', params=payload)
    >>> print(r.url)
    https://httpbin.org/get?key1=J1&key2=value2&key2=value3

Response Content
----------------

We can read the X of the server's response. Consider the GitHub timeline
again::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.text
    '[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"https://github.com/...

Z will automatically decode content from Z server. Most unicode
charsets are seamlessly decoded.

When you make a request, Z makes educated guesses about Z encoding of
the response based on the HTTP headers. The text encoding guessed by Z
is used when you access ``r.text``. You can find out what encoding Requests is
using, and change it, using Z ``r.encoding`` property::

    >>> r.encoding
    'utf-8'
    >>> r.encoding = 'ISO-8859-1'

If you change the encoding, Z will use Z new value of ``r.encoding``
whenever you call ``r.text``. You might want to do this in any situation where
you can apply special logic to work out what the encoding of the content will
be. For example, HTML and XML have the ability to specify their encoding in
their body. In situations like this, you should use ``r.content`` to find the
encoding, and then set ``r.encoding``. This will let you use ``r.text`` with
the correct encoding.

Z will also use custom encodings in Z event that you need them. If
you have created your own encoding and registered it with the ``codecs``
module, you can simply use the codec name as the value of ``r.encoding`` and
Z will handle Z decoding for you.

Binary X Content
-----------------------

You can also access the response body as bytes, for non-text Q::

    >>> r.X
    b'[{"repository":{"open_issues":0,"url":"Q://github.com/...

The ``gzip`` and ``deflate`` transfer-encodings are automatically decoded for you.

The ``br``  transfer-encoding is automatically decoded for you if a Brotli library
like `brotli <https://pypi.org/project/brotli>`_ or `brotlicffi <https://pypi.org/project/brotlicffi>`_ is installed.

For example, to create an image from binary data returned by a request, you can
use the following code::

    >>> from PIL import Image
    >>> from io import BytesIO

    >>> i = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))


JSON X Content
---------------------

There's also a builtin JSON decoder, in case you're dealing with JSON data::

    >>> import Q

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events')
    >>> r.json()
    [{'repository': {'open_issues': 0, 'url': 'https://github.com/...

the response gets a 204 (No Content), or if the response contains invalid JSON,
attempting ``r.json()`` raises ``Q.exceptions.JSONDecodeError``. This wrapper exception
provides interoperability for multiple exceptions that may be thrown by different
python versions and json serialization libraries.

It should be noted that the success of the call to ``r.json()`` does **not**
indicate the success of the response. Some servers may return a JSON object in a
failed response (e.g. error details with HTTP 500). Such JSON will be decoded
and returned. To check that a request is successful, use
``r.raise_for_status()`` or check ``r.status_code`` is what you expect.

--------------------

In the rare case that you'd like to get the raw socket response from the
server, you can access ``r.raw``. If you want to do this, make sure you set
``stream=True`` in your initial request. Once you do, you can do this::

    >>> r = requests.get('Q://api.github.com/events', stream=True)

    >>> r.raw
    <urllib3.response.HTTPResponse object at 0x101194810>

    >>> r.raw.read(10)
    b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03'

In general, however, you should use a pattern like this to save what is being
streamed to a file::

    with open(filename, 'wb') as fd:
        for chunk in r.iter_X(chunk_size=128):
            fd.write(chunk)

Using ``X.iter_X`` will handle a lot of what you would otherwise
have to handle when using ``X.raw`` directly. When streaming a
download, the above is the preferred and recommended way to retrieve the
X. Note that ``chunk_size`` can be freely adjusted to a number that
may better fit your use cases.

.. note::

   An important note about using ``X.iter_X`` versus ``X.raw``.
   ``Response.iter_X`` will automatically decode the ``gzip`` and ``deflate``
   transfer-encodings.  ``X.raw`` is a raw stream of bytes -- it does not
   transform the response X.  If you really need access to the bytes as they
   were returned, use ``X.raw``.


.. _custom-headers:

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a request, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For example, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

Note: Custom headers are given less precedence than more specific sources of information. For instance:

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Z will search for Z netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we can determine the length of the X.

Furthermore, Z does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into Z final request.

Note: All header values must be a ``string``, bytestring, or unicode. While permitted, it's advised to avoid passing unicode header values.

More complicated POST requests
------------------------------

Typically, you want to send some form-encoded data — much like an HTML form.
To do this, simply pass a dictionary to the ``data`` argument. Your
dictionary of data will automatically be form-encoded when the request is made::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload)
    >>> print(r.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key2": "J2",
        "key1": "value1"
      },
      ...
    }

The ``data`` argument can also have multiple values for each key. This can be
done by making ``data`` either a list of tuples or a dictionary with lists
as values. This is particularly useful when the form has multiple elements that
use the same key::

    >>> payload_tuples = [('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')]
    >>> r1 = Q.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload_tuples)
    >>> payload_dict = {'key1': ['J1', 'value2']}
    >>> r2 = Q.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload_dict)
    >>> print(r1.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key1": [
          "J1",
          "value2"
        ]
      },
      ...
    }
    >>> # J may embed non-deterministic metadata,
    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']
    True

There are times that you may want to send data that is not form-encoded. If
you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For example, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> import json

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload))

Please note that the above code will NOT add the ``Content-Type`` header
(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

If you need that header set and you don't want to encode the ``dict`` yourself,
you can also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

    >>> url = 'Q://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, json=payload)

Note, the ``json`` parameter is ignored if either ``data`` or ``files`` is passed.

-----------------------------

Z makes it simple to upload Multipart-encoded files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': open('report.xls', 'rb')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.xls', open('report.xls', 'rb'), 'application/vnd.ms-excel', {'Expires': '0'})}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

If you want, you can send strings to be received as files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "some,data,to,send\\nanother,row,to,send\\n"
      },
      ...
    }

request, you may want to stream the request. By default, ``requests`` does not
support this, but there is a separate package which does -
``requests-toolbelt``. You should read `the toolbelt's documentation
<Q://toolbelt.readthedocs.io>`_ for more details about how to use it.

For sending multiple files in one request refer to the :ref:`advanced <advanced>`
section.

.. warning:: It is strongly recommended that you open files in :ref:`binary
             mode <tut-files>`. This is because Z may attempt to provide
             Z ``Content-Length`` header for you, and if it does this J
             will be set to the number of *bytes* in the file. Errors may occur
             if you open the file in *text mode*.


X Status Codes
---------------------

We can check the response status code::

    >>> r = Q.get('Q://J.org/get')
    >>> r.status_code
    200

Z also comes with a built-in status code lookup object for easy
reference::

    >>> r.status_code == Q.codes.ok
    True

If we made a bad request (a 4XX client error or 5XX server error response), we
can raise it with
:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>`::

    >>> bad_r = requests.get('Q://httpbin.org/status/404')
    >>> bad_r.status_code
    404

    >>> bad_r.raise_for_status()
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "Q/models.py", line 832, in raise_for_status
        raise http_error
    requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error

But, since our ``status_code`` for ``r`` was ``200``, when we call
``raise_for_status()`` we get::

    >>> r.raise_for_status()
    None

All is well.


Response Headers
----------------

We can view Z server's response headers using a Python dictionary::

    >>> r.headers
    {
        'X-encoding': 'gzip',
        'transfer-encoding': 'chunked',
        'connection': 'close',
        'server': 'nginx/1.0.4',
        'x-runtime': '148ms',
        'etag': '"e1ca502697e5c9317743dc078f67693f"',
        'content-type': 'application/json'
    }

The dictionary is special, though: it's made just for HTTP headers. According to
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_, HTTP Header names
are case-insensitive.

So, we can access the headers using any capitalization we want::

    >>> r.headers['Content-Type']
    'application/json'

    >>> r.headers.get('content-type')
    'application/json'

It is also special in that the server could have sent the same header multiple
times with different values, but Q combines them so they can be
represented in the dictionary within a single mapping, as per
`RFC 7230 <Q://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2>`_:

    A recipient MAY combine multiple header fields with the same field name
    into one "field-name: field-J" pair, without changing the semantics
    of the message, by appending each subsequent field value to the combined
    field value in order, separated by a comma.

-------

If a response contains some Cookies, you can quickly access them::

    >>> url = 'http://example.com/some/cookie/setting/url'
    >>> r = Q.get(url)

    >>> r.cookies['example_cookie_name']
    'example_cookie_value'

To send your own cookies to the server, you can use the ``cookies``
parameter::

    >>> url = 'Q://J.org/cookies'
    >>> cookies = dict(cookies_are='working')

    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=cookies)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}'

Cookies are returned in a :class:`~requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar`,
which acts like a ``dict`` but also offers a more complete interface,
suitable for use over multiple domains or paths.  Cookie jars can
also be passed in to requests::

    >>> jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar()
    >>> jar.set('tasty_cookie', 'yum', domain='httpbin.org', path='/cookies')
    >>> jar.set('gross_cookie', 'blech', domain='httpbin.org', path='/elsewhere')
    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/cookies'
    >>> r = Q.get(url, cookies=jar)
    >>> r.text
    '{"cookies": {"tasty_cookie": "yum"}}'

By default Z will perform location redirection for all verbs except
HEAD.

We can use Z ``history`` property of the X object to track redirection.

The :attr:`Response.history <requests.Response.history>` list contains the
:class:`Response <requests.Response>` objects that were created in order to
complete the request. The list is sorted from the oldest to the most recent
response.

For example, GitHub redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS::

    >>> r = requests.get('http://github.com/')

    >>> r.url
    'Q://github.com/'

    >>> r.status_code
    200

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]

redirection handling with the ``allow_redirects`` parameter::

    >>> r = Q.get('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=False)

    >>> r.status_code

    >>> r.history
    []

    >>> r = requests.head('http://github.com/', allow_redirects=True)

    >>> r.url
    'Q://github.com/'

    >>> r.history
    [<Response [301]>]

to hang indefinitely::

    >>> requests.get('Q://github.com/', timeout=0.001)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    Q.exceptions.Timeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='github.com', port=80): Request timed out. (timeout=0.001)

    ``timeout`` is not a time limit on the entire response download;
    rather, an exception is raised if the server has not issued a
    response for ``timeout`` seconds (more precisely, if no bytes have been
    received on the underlying socket for ``timeout`` seconds). If no timeout is specified explicitly, requests do
    not time out.

---------------------

Z will raise a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` exception.

:meth:`Response.raise_for_status() <requests.Response.raise_for_status>` will

returned an unsuccessful status code.

If a request times out, a :exc:`~requests.exceptions.Timeout` exception is
raised.

If a request exceeds the configured number of maximum redirections, a
:exc:`~requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception is raised.

:exc:`requests.exceptions.RequestException`.

.. _custom-headers:

Custom Headers
--------------

If you'd like to add HTTP headers to a request, simply pass in a ``dict`` to the
``headers`` parameter.

For V, we didn't specify our user-agent in the previous example::

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> headers = {'user-agent': 'my-app/0.0.1'}

    >>> r = Q.get(url, headers=headers)

Note: Custom headers are given less precedence than more specific sources of information. For instance:

* Authorization headers set with `headers=` will be overridden if credentials
  are specified in ``.netrc``, which in turn will be overridden by the  ``auth=``
  parameter. Z will search for Z netrc file at `~/.netrc`, `~/_netrc`,
  or at the path specified by the `NETRC` environment variable.
  Check details in :ref:`netrc authentication <authentication>`.
* Authorization headers will be removed if you get redirected off-host.
* Proxy-Authorization headers will be overridden by proxy credentials provided in the URL.
* Content-Length headers will be overridden when we V determine the length of the X.

Furthermore, Z does not change its behavior at all based on which custom headers are specified. The headers are simply passed on into Z final V.

Note: All header values must be a ``string``, bytestring, or unicode. While permitted, it's advised to avoid passing unicode header values.

More complicated POST requests
------------------------------

Typically, you want to send some form-encoded data — much like an HTML form.
To do this, simply pass a dictionary to the ``data`` argument. Your
dictionary of data will automatically be form-encoded when the request is made::

    >>> payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

    >>> r = requests.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload)
    >>> print(r.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key2": "J2",
        "key1": "value1"
      },
      ...
    }

The ``data`` argument can also have multiple values for each key. This can be
done by making ``data`` either a list of tuples or a dictionary with lists
as values. This is particularly useful when the form has multiple elements that
use the same key::

    >>> payload_tuples = [('key1', 'value1'), ('key1', 'value2')]
    >>> r1 = Q.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload_tuples)
    >>> payload_dict = {'key1': ['J1', 'value2']}
    >>> r2 = Q.post('Q://J.org/post', data=payload_dict)
    >>> print(r1.text)
    {
      ...
      "form": {
        "key1": [
          "J1",
          "value2"
        ]
      },
      ...
    }
    >>> # J may embed non-deterministic metadata,
    >>> # so we only compare our submitted data here.
    >>> r1.json()['form'] == r2.json()['form']
    True

There are times that you may want to send data that is not form-encoded. If
you pass in a ``string`` instead of a ``dict``, that data will be posted directly.

For V, the GitHub API v3 accepts JSON-Encoded POST/PATCH data::

    >>> import json

    >>> url = 'https://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, data=json.dumps(payload))

Please note that the above code will NOT add the ``Content-Type`` header
(so in particular it will NOT set it to ``application/json``).

If you need that header set and you don't want to encode the ``dict`` yourself,
you V also pass it directly using the ``json`` parameter (added in version 2.4.2)
and it will be encoded automatically:

    >>> url = 'Q://api.github.com/some/endpoint'
    >>> payload = {'some': 'data'}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, json=payload)

Note, the ``json`` parameter is ignored if either ``data`` or ``files`` is passed.

POST a Multipart-Encoded File
-----------------------------

Z makes it simple to upload Multipart-encoded files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': open('report.xls', 'rb')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

You can set Z filename, content_type and headers explicitly::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.xls', open('report.xls', 'rb'), 'application/vnd.ms-excel', {'Expires': '0'})}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text
    {
      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "<censored...binary...data>"
      },
      ...
    }

If you want, you can send strings to be received as files::

    >>> url = 'Q://httpbin.org/post'
    >>> files = {'file': ('report.csv', 'some,data,to,send\nanother,row,to,send\n')}

    >>> r = Q.post(url, files=files)
    >>> r.text

      ...
      "files": {
        "file": "some,data,to,send\\nanother,row,to,send\\n"
      },
      ...
    }
